title: The Olympic Games: seven short texts
texts: Soon after the Second World War, a doctor organised a modest archery contest for wounded soldiers at a hospital, believing that competition could restore confidence as well as strength. The idea soon outgrew the hospital lawn. Today the Paralympics are a major event in their own right, where athletes ask for admiration rather than sympathy, and adapted rules and equipment ensure that nobody is excluded because of a physical difference.

Long before stadiums and sponsors, the Greeks gathered at Olympia every four years. Conflicts between cities did not end, but messengers carried word of a sacred truce from state to state, and travellers on their way to the games were promised safe passage; anyone who attacked them risked a heavy fine. Winners received only a wreath of olive leaves, yet the custom survived for over a thousand years.

Every city bidding for the Games pledges a lasting benefit, and some deliver: one Spanish city opened up its seafront and a London district gained a park. Elsewhere, stadiums built at enormous expense stand almost empty, and taxpayers go on paying long after the closing ceremony. Supporters stress tourism and civic pride, while critics point out that the final bill is almost always larger than the figure announced at the start.

Visitors from any country can read the Games without a guide: five interlocking rings for the continents, and a flame passed from hand to hand across the world. Many assume the relay is as old as the festival itself; in fact it was invented for the 1936 Games. Whatever language people speak, these signs say the same thing, and no barrier of speech can blur a shared hope.

A festival that depends on television audiences cannot ignore the habits of younger viewers, which explains why skateboarding, surfing and climbing arrived in Tokyo, and breaking, a form of street dance, in Paris. Traditionalists grumble that such additions cheapen the Games; organisers reply that an event which never changed would quietly die. After all, the list of sports has been adjusted from one cycle to the next since the earliest days.

After a pause of some fifteen centuries, a French educator persuaded doubtful officials that the ancient contests could be revived and might bring young people from rival nations closer together. The first modern Games took place in Athens in 1896, with only fourteen countries and no women, who were newcomers to the programme at the second Games, four years later.

The winter edition of the Games began in a French mountain town in 1924, a sequel to the summer festival, with a handful of sports and modest crowds. Its programme has grown steadily, and snowboarding, dismissed by purists as a passing fashion, joined in the 1990s. Because it depends on snow and ice, the event needs costly mountain venues, increasingly exposed to warm winters.
discuss: Do you think the Olympic Games are still relevant today? Why or why not?
Should new sports such as skateboarding or breaking be part of the Olympic programme?
Would your city benefit from hosting the Games? What would be the main advantages and disadvantages?
